items.title: A remote employee refused 160 webcam photos a day. Her employer fired her
items.summary:
Across the workforce, employer surveillance is growing increasingly common, even though it is widely disliked by employees. According to the  American Psychological Association , employee monitoring increases workers’ stress and decreases their reported mental health. A Canadian study found that surveillance in the workplace makes employees feel more pressured, less satisfied with their job, and like their privacy is being violated.

AI may now make this problem worse. These negative outcomes are the consequences of more traditional surveillance methods like keyboard tracking and email monitoring. Considering that, what would the psychological impact be of learning that an employer will now use AI to take 160 photos of an employee’s face every day?

A recent New Jersey lawsuit alleges that an employer was trying to do just that, and fired its employee when she refused to agree to this monitoring. The plaintiff in this case, Glennis Von Sander-Timinski, worked for Sutherland Healthcare Solutions, which provides healthcare services outsourcing. The suit states that she had been working at home with no issues since 2018, and had achieved positive performance reviews during that time. 

However, everything changed in August when her company told her that they would be using a new tool: Sentinel AI. This software would take a photo of her through her webcam about every three minutes over the course of the day, for a total of about 160 photos per day.

Von Sander-Timinski objected to this with the worry that it would increase her stress level, and therefore trigger her…
items.t: A remote employee refused 160 webcam photos a day. Her employer fired her

items.title: Microsoft’s massive outage puts its AI-driven layoffs under scrutiny
items.summary:
Microsoft’s massive service outage on Thursday left businesses and government agencies scrambling to access critical services. It also came at an awkward moment for the tech giant, which has undertaken an extensive initiative to reduce its workforce even as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence .

Recent efforts to trim the company’s head count included extending buyout offers to 9,000 U.S. employees in April and 60,000 employees in four countries in October . It also laid off 4,800 workers in July, mostly in its sales and Xbox divisions. Last month, The Information also reported that leadership in Microsoft’s Azure cloud division had discussed cutting costs by at least 20%; Microsoft denied the report .

Meanwhile, the company is pouring billions into AI infrastructure. Earlier this year, it projected roughly $190 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, much of it driven by the enormous computing demands of AI and cloud services.

Fast Company has reached out to Microsoft for comment.

There is no evidence that either the workforce reductions or AI investments directly contributed to Thursday’s disruption. But the incident raises a broader question for Microsoft and the tech industry: As businesses shrink their workforces and increasingly rely on AI to boost productivity , are they also risking the reliability of their existing products? 

Workforce reductions and restructurings can push out experienced employees who understand how a company’s systems work , including any longtime bugs or quirks, and who know how to respond when something breaks.…
items.t: Microsoft’s massive outage puts its AI-driven layoffs under scrutiny

items.title: The first and last 3 minutes: How great storytellers win and keep attention
items.summary:
Think about the last business presentation you attended. Chances are the speaker spent hours preparing slides, polishing statistics, and rehearsing the main points. But how did the presentation begin? With a lengthy introduction, a list of credentials, or a few words thanking everyone for attending?

Those opening moments may have cost the speaker the audience’s attention before the presentation even began, and that speaker may have lost the opportunity to make a lasting impression.

After years of speaking to audiences of all sizes, I’ve learned that the first and last three minutes of a presentation deserve more thought than almost anything in between. The opening earns your audience’s attention, while the ending determines what they remember and what they do next.

Your Audience Decides Faster Than You Think 

Why the first three minutes? Audiences will decide almost instantly whether to continue giving you their attention or start tuning you out. That’s why I consider the first three minutes—roughly 350 to 400 words at a typical speaking pace—so critical. Your opening must give listeners a reason to keep listening.

An effective opening creates a reason for your audience to stay with you and lean in for more. A strong opening statement can start with something unexpected, a moment of conflict or confusion, a startling discovery, or an intriguing line of dialogue. Your goal is to make your audience want to hear the next sentence.

One of my favorite examples is the story of Dick Hoyt, who refused to give up on his son Rick, born with spastic quadriplegia. When I tell…
items.t: The first and last 3 minutes: How great storytellers win and keep attention

items.title: Kalshi will pay you $120,000 to play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
items.summary:
People are already calling out sick to play the feverishly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI . Companies like Logitech are even giving staff paid time off to partake. 

Now, thanks to prediction market Kalshi, folks won’t have to play hooky from their jobs to dive into the video game—the first installment in 13 years of Rockstar Games’ hit franchise that has earned the company billions worldwide. Instead, one person can make playing it their literal job.

Kalshi will pay a lucky gamer between $100,000 and $120,000 to play Grand Theft Auto VI ’s story mode through to completion, starting right at midnight on launch day, November 19. The ideal candidate is “an experienced gamer” and “streamer with your own channel,” the listing states, along with “18+ years of life IRL, 10+ years of sweaty gaming, 3+ years of streaming experience.” They’ll get an extra $15,000 upon completion of the project.

As Kalshi’s “researcher”—and yes, per the LinkedIn post, the company assures that this is a real job—the winning candidate will be tasked with exploring and studying Leonida’s in-game economy of robberies and heists, perfecting the “optimal moneymaking strategy” and building “a spreadsheet to prove it,” to the point where they’ll get “accused of ruining the game for everyone else.”

items.title: CEOs still think they can get away with affairs after #MeToo
items.summary:
Nearly a decade after the #MeToo movement burst into public consciousness , the upheaval at Nvidia may be a lesson in how little CEOs seem to have learned. 

Nvidia’s embattled CEO, Jensen Huang, has resigned following a New York Times report on Wednesday that revealed he had engaged in another extramarital relationship—this time involving a subordinate, the company’s vice president of healthcare and one of his 60 direct reports. The affair was a blatant violation of Nvidia’s code of conduct , which notes that employees should steer clear of situations that could create a conflict of interest, including “personal relationships.” The company also purports to “promptly investigate” reports of misconduct.

While this dalliance has fewer national security implications than his entanglement with an alleged Chinese spy , it does suggest that CEOs like Huang don’t expect to face consequences for getting involved with employees. 

Huang is in good company: Many employers have similar policies that forbid romantic relationships between managers and their direct reports, but that hasn’t stopped executives from crossing the line anyway. (Who could forget the viral video of the Astronomer CEO caught canoodling with his chief people officer at a Coldplay concert ?)

In recent years, however, a number of executives have been forced to step down after pursuing inappropriate relationships, in addition to CEOs like Leslie Moonves (formerly head of CBS) being fired for sexual harassment. 

Back in 2019, McDonald’s then-CEO Steve Easterbrook was ousted over a relationship with a subordinate.…
items.t: CEOs still think they can get away with affairs after #MeToo

items.title: Can we please stop calling it a ‘honey trap’?
items.summary:
When Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on November 8 that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife , there’s a phrase that quickly became omnipresent in the media: Huang had been the victim of a “honey trap,” laid by Alice Huang (no relation), a Singapore-based tech executive identified as a Chinese spy by U.S. intelligence agencies.

“Honey trap,” seriously?

The story behind the phrase, a longstanding term of art in spy craft, is that a good, hardworking man was minding his own business when a serpent of a woman lured him off the righteous path by dishonest means and propositions he, being a man, simply couldn’t refuse. It is assumed that male sex drive is some kind of force of nature that no adult can reasonably be expected to control.

So there’s a double sexist stereotype here. Can a 63-year-old billionaire CEO really be supposed to have no say over his sex life? Like a bear wouldn’t be able to resist honey?

Anyone who, like me, grew up in the 1980s knows a close relative of this idea: the “homewrecker,” a word aimed at the other woman and never at the husband who cheated. One of the decade’s most successful films, Fatal Attraction (1987), tells the story of a married man (Michael Douglas) whose affair turns into a nightmare when the woman (Glenn Close) refuses to stay discreet and starts asking for more. The film portrays the mistress as mentally unstable and dangerous. The film ends with the wife killing the mistress and family values restored. The husband’s betrayal is never really an issue. I’m ashamed to admit that when I first watched it, some time in the 1990s, I…
items.t: Can we please stop calling it a ‘honey trap’?

items.title: Burnout is a workplace safety hazard. It’s time to start treating it like one
items.summary:
Burnout is a huge workplace issue: the low engagement that comes with it costs every business affected a fortune. Worse yet, its effects on workers are deleterious to the point where it can literally lead to death.

Yet in my experience, most leaders consider “burnout” an HR line item to be managed by a wellness program. It’s hard to know how to jolt people out of this mindset, but if I were a CEO (and I am), I’d be very concerned about potential industrial manslaughter charges coming my way at worst, and shareholders rightfully wondering why I am failing to manage the main thing that’s materially impairing productivity at best.

Burnout is a workplace safety hazard—and needs to be governed as one. 

The World Health Organization  defines burnout  as the result of “chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.” It’s a costly hazard that claims at least twice as many lives as workplace accidents. Long working hours alone led to an estimated 750,000 deaths from stroke and heart disease in 2016, more than twice the 360,000 people killed by workplace injuries,  according to a report  from WHO and the International Labour Organization. In the USA, workplace stressors are estimated  to kill 120,000 people a year . 

Outside of the devastating human impact, the toll burnout takes on commercial performance should be triggering emergency board meetings all over the world. At an estimated cost of US $5 million a year for a company of 1,000 employees , it would be reasonable to ask very direct questions of the executive about their plans to arrest the poorly…
items.t: Burnout is a workplace safety hazard. It’s time to start treating it like one

items.title: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
‘I look out for my team,’ a store manager tells me, but Poundland’s US owner doesn’t care. Labour may be too late to prevent it becoming yet another casualty of venture capital

In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains.

On Tuesday £10m was released: not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.t: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets | Polly Toynbee

items.title: What I let AI touch in my solo business—and what stays off-limits
items.summary:
A lot of AI advice suggests that you hand over work to a personal agent, like letting it triage your inbox or shop for you. That’s certainly appealing, since we’re all relentlessly busy and constantly fighting small tasks that take up our time. 

But every time you connect an AI tool to one of your accounts, you’re also answering a second question: What is this tool allowed to do on my behalf? 

For a lot of solopreneurs, that question gets answered by default. You click “allow” on the permissions screen, and the tool can now reach everything in that account. 

I use AI a lot in my business, but I’ve also drawn some very clear boundaries around what it can access.

Sort your tools by what AI can do in them 

Every AI tool I use falls into one of three buckets.

Read but not edit. AI can pull information from the tool, but it can’t change anything. This works well for reference material you want AI to draw from without any risk of it being rewritten.

One example, for me, is pulling financial data from QuickBooks. I let Claude analyze some numbers every month, but I don’t want AI making changes to my transactions.

Full editing. AI can create and change things directly in these tools. This makes sense where a mistake is easy to spot and quick to undo.

I use Canva to plan a lot of my marketing material. Nothing is mission-critical, and the full ability to make changes gives me a lot of capabilities to use Claude with Canva.

Off-limits. AI can’t access the tool at all. 

One thing I don’t let AI touch at all is my bank accounts. JP Morgan Chase reported that people were…
items.t: What I let AI touch in my solo business—and what stays off-limits

items.title: What it’s like to change careers when you’re at the top of your game
items.summary:
When Kim Foster was 17, she decided she was going to become a doctor. 

It was a feat that no one in her family had accomplished. “I just strapped in and did what I needed to do to execute on that big goal,” she says. Foster worked toward getting into medical school, graduating, and all the subsequent training. Then she practiced medicine for 20 years. “It was great for a while,” she says, “until it wasn’t anymore.” 

During the last few years as a family doctor, Foster noticed a pattern. She was often seeing patients when they were already experiencing problems—diabetes, chronic pain, heart disease. By the time they got in front of her, she says, “things were starting to fall apart.” 

She began to feel a pull toward helping people make different decisions, and also yearned to do something creative. Eventually, she decided to walk away from her medical career. Now the 54-year-old helps those who are looking to make pivots or reinvent themselves in their lives through her YouTube channel and online courses . 

Outgrowing your established career later in life 

Like Foster, Alexandra Aileru knows what it’s like to outgrow one’s career. The 35-year-old had worked in the education sector for eight years. She’d already been thinking about leaving her field for a while. Then she became pregnant and realized she needed to make an exit. 

Aileru transitioned into project management before realizing a few years in that she’d hit what she calls the peak of what she wanted to achieve in that role. At the end of 2023, she started posting on TikTok about her career pivot experience.…
items.t: What it’s like to change careers when you’re at the top of your game

items.title: Why PTO in the U.S. is so unbelievably bad
items.summary:
Most countries around the world offer workers some form of paid time off (PTO). So, how did the U.S. become one of the few outliers that has no federally guaranteed paid vacation, maternity, family, or bereavement leave—let alone sick time? 

The factors are many, ranging from cultural expectations to legal ones. In America, PTO is up to the employer or local officials, rather than treated as something every working person deserves.

“I think that has shaped how we view time off,” says Cory McCruden, CEO of Best Upon Request, a concierge service focused on employee well-being. “It can feel like a benefit your employer gives you rather than a normal part of working and living.”

PTO is certainly a privilege for workers in the U.S. That reality makes life harder for everyone, from the parent who needs to leave work early to pick up a child to the individual who woke up with the flu. Thanksgiving’s just around the corner, and while it’s a federal holiday, many workers may feel anxious about asking for extra time off . A single day is hardly generous, especially when traveling to see family can be so time-consuming.

The current situation comes in spite of the fact that taking PTO has been proven to improve employee retention —increasing with the number of days off—and offer psychological benefits to the individual . 

So, why is the state of PTO in America so bad? Things have gone wrong to get to this point, but there could be ways to turn it around.

Again, PTO is not nationally guaranteed in any form.

items.t: Why PTO in the U.S. is so unbelievably bad

items.title: This company is giving workers time off to play the new ‘Grand Theft Auto’
items.summary:
With the highly anticipated release of Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI just around the corner, one company is unveiling a new perk for its employees: paid time off for gaming.

In an initiative it’s calling “Logi Game Day,” consumer electronics firm Logitech announced Tuesday that each of its 7,000 workers will receive one paid day off per year to play video games.

Along with hosting a streaming event at its Americas headquarters in San Jose on November 19, the company says it is “formally recognizing the cognitive and professional benefits of gaming.”

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” said CEO Hanneke Faber. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.”

It’s no coincidence that Logi Game Day falls on the same day as one of the most-hyped video game releases in recent memory. Grand Theft Auto VI is the first new title in the best-selling series in 13 years, and many workers are already planning on catching “GTA flu” to make the most of release day. 

In one survey of 1,000 U.S. adults who work full-time and regularly play video games, 39% said they planned to request time off in advance to play the game, 36% said they planned to call in sick on release day, and 32% said they would work from home.

The Wall Street Journal has already warned of a “ work blackout ,” and a Spanish economist has estimated that the release of GTA VI could cost the U.S. $1 billion in lost productivity .

Clearly, Logitech is unbothered by such concerns. The company,…

items.title: Dads want to do more caregiving. But here’s how workplaces hold them back
items.summary:
The tension between caregiving obligations and work responsibilities is often framed as a women’s issue. But it’s not just working mothers who find themselves in a bind: Plenty of men say they not only value caregiving but want to do more of it. So what’s holding them back?

A new report from the Better Life Lab at the think tank New America—which publishes research on workplace equity and family policy—indicates that men face some of the same hurdles that working women do, from limited flexibility or autonomy to a lack of structural support. 

Compared with 2019, men are taking more time off from work or reducing their work hours due to caregiving responsibilities, especially those who earn less or have children with special needs. At the same time, they continue to grapple with the kind of cultural stigma that can keep them from taking paid leave even when they’re entitled to it. 

The report’s findings suggest that many men actually want to spend more time on caregiving. In fact, a surprising number of fathers—6 in 10—expressed an interest in staying home full time. Men who helped care for adults or children with special needs were even more interested in being home. Over two-thirds of the men surveyed claim to think caregiving is as important as paid work, and that both parents should contribute equally. But the reality is quite different: Only about 40% of respondents who are caregivers and parents said they actually split those responsibilities equally.  

There are a number of potential explanations for this disparity. Over a quarter of dads said there are barriers…
items.t: Dads want to do more caregiving. But here’s how workplaces hold them back

items.title: People can’t stop trolling AI job ‘interviewers’
items.summary:
AI is conducting job interviews more and more widely . And while it may be anxiety-inducing for some—as they attempt to figure out what a robot deems hirable—others are rage-baiting the technology for the lolz in skits online.

In one recent viral video shared to X, content creator Nick Reid hilariously trolled his AI interviewer, “Karen,” who was seemingly screening him for a job at Burger King—one he clearly didn’t want. 

Mind you, Karen isn’t a real BK “employee”: ”We do not use, nor are we aware of any Franchisee across the U.S. or Canada using a tool like this,” Burger King told Fast Company in a comment. But the comedy skit still highlights how awkward interacting with AI bots can be. 

And for viewers fed up with the AI revolution, it may be more than a little cathartic to watch .

In the video, which has racked up nearly 8 million views, Reid appears shirtless and with a shoe on his head and introduces himself as Crangeus McBasketball. “Why on Earth do you have a shoe on your head?” Karen replies, while he laughs in her face.

Mr. McBasketball continues to mock the AI by telling it he’s extremely busy and responding to its questions in more and more ridiculous ways. When the AI asks if he would be able to reliably get to shifts at the restaurant, he responds by saying, “Yeah. I have feet.” Karen’s not having it: “That is an incredibly odd way to answer a simple question.” 

But this isn’t the only corner of the internet in which “jobseekers” are taking the mickey out of AI avatars. In another video shared to LinkedIn, a man trolls his AI interviewer by speaking…
items.t: People can’t stop trolling AI job ‘interviewers’

items.title: Your next great hire might have a military résumé
items.summary:
How many military veterans has your company hired in the past five years? And how many of those hires came from actively recruiting veterans rather than simply waiting for them to apply?

I’ve spent more than 30 years helping companies find talent, and I know how easy it is to rule out good candidates when their backgrounds don’t exactly match what a hiring manager expects.

Military veterans are a good example. They’ve spent years developing practical skills, but getting employers to recognize how those skills translate to civilian jobs can be an uphill battle.

In fact, while 69% of U.S. employers report difficulty finding qualified talent, many veterans are struggling to find work that makes full use of their experience. According to Indeed and The Harris Poll, 57% of veterans surveyed felt underemployed or believed their jobs underrepresented their military responsibilities.

Some of the people you’re looking for could already have years of relevant experience, even if their résumés don’t look quite like what you’re used to seeing.

4 ways to tap into overlooked veteran talent 

I’ve worked with plenty of employers who want to hire veterans but aren’t sure how to evaluate their military experience. A few changes to how you approach recruiting and hiring make a real difference.

1. Understand the experience behind military job titles 

Our team at Orion Talent helped place a Navy pilot in a service area manager position at a medical imaging company. On paper, he probably wasn’t the candidate you’d expect to oversee technicians who install and repair MRI and CT equipment…
items.t: Your next great hire might have a military résumé

items.title: Open enrollment is squeezing small businesses. Nearly 70% want outside help
items.summary:
With businesses now overseeing open enrollment for their workers, many employers admit they’re struggling to find ways to finance and organize increasingly complex  benefit plans . Yet rather than decide to simply cut  those programs  as too costly and laborious to continue, a majority of  small business owners  are considering turning to outside experts’ help to make them more effective.

Employers’ commitment to benefits, and accompanying awareness that their plans are getting too difficult to operate alone, were two major findings in a  recent survey  of 759 small businesses by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce (USCC) and JustWorks, an HR tech company. Nearly 70% of participating entrepreneurs said they recognize they need help in running their programs, and “wish they had outside” support in structuring, operating, and budgeting them. That desire for expert third-party assistance stood at 75% among Gen Z and millennial owners, with 64% and 54% of Gen Xers and boomers considering the idea, respectively.

Little wonder so many entrepreneurs are considering outside help in orchestrating benefits programs—especially with annual open enrollment activity underway. In addition to managing the often wide array of options included in many company plans, business owners are also forced to find new budgeting adjustments to fund their rising costs.

Health care insurance is the main example of that. While premium increases to all companies this year are slated to surpass 9%, they’re hitting small businesses particularly hard.

Despite rising costs, owners expand benefit coverage…
items.t: Open enrollment is squeezing small businesses. Nearly 70% want outside help

items.title: Gen Zers and millennials are rapidly taking advantage of this health insurance tip for freelancers
items.summary:
When Madelyn Roman, 31, wanted to go freelance , the biggest barrier she faced wasn’t how she would make money, but how she would afford healthcare. 

Like many people in the U.S., Roman’s health insurance was tied to her employer. But then she learned about a way to get health insurance through her fiancé. (And no, it wasn’t pushing forward the wedding.)

Once a common method for same-sex couples to gain basic rights previously denied to them but long associated with “traditional” marriage, ranging from shared healthcare to inheritance, couples of all sexual orientations are now entering domestic partnerships as a precursor—or alternative—to marriage. 

In the U.S., domestic partnerships can offer benefits such as access to a partner’s employee healthcare, hospital visitation rights, and veteran’s benefits. 

For New York City-based Roman, that right to healthcare can be life-changing. And she’s not alone. According to FlexJobs , there are 72 million independent workers in the U.S., a number that is expected to rise to 86.5 million next year. 

“As a healthcare professional myself, I’ve always taken advantage of my insurance plan,” she says. “I need it for both my physical and mental healthcare services, which I rely on. Life is too unpredictable to go without coverage. Now I have so much freedom to do what I want to do and to work how I want to work.”

items.title: Most solopreneurs turn to AI before hiring others, data suggests. Here’s why
items.summary:
Going out on your own and starting a business can be daunting. Every decision feels heavy. You quickly realize that each role within your company—accountant, marketer, customer service, salesperson—belongs only to you. You have to handle tasks you didn’t even know existed. As your business grows more successful, the tasks keep growing.

Years ago, there was one clear solution: hire more people. Bring on team members to take on the work. But today, solopreneurs are taking a different course of action. Now, according to our research at cloud-based accounting software company Freshbooks,  86% of solopreneurs and micro-business owners  will turn to AI before hiring outside help. And it makes sense: it can save time and energy and allow these entrepreneurs to focus on the most important parts of scaling their businesses. At the same time, there are still places where AI usage falls short, and it’s necessary to hire or look for outside support.

AI solves the startup challenges 

According to solopreneurs, the biggest area where AI supports them is the initial building phase of creating a business. Ninety percent say that AI made it easier to build and run a business as one person. After all, there are only so many hours in the day, and AI can take some of the more tedious tasks off of a  solopreneur’s ever-growing to-do list .

AI can manage scheduling and calendars. It can create first drafts of social posts and marketing materials. It can do the heavy lifting of building a website and creating early business plans. With AI, solopreneurs are finding ways to do it all and build…
items.t: Most solopreneurs turn to AI before hiring others, data suggests. Here’s why

items.title: Stocks, bonds, and cash: How to strike the right balance with your assets
items.summary:
With cash and bond yields at their highest levels in over 15 years, many investors wonder if they should favor these higher-yielding options over stocks.

Here are answers to some questions investors might have about how to approach asset allocation in an era of 5% CD yields.

What’s the problem with holding extra cash? 

The yields on cash products are compelling today, and cash investors do not have the potential for principal volatility. That’s particularly appealing because we’ve seen losses for some bond investors over the past few years and so far in 2026. Additionally, our annual diversification research has shown that cash is a solid diversifier for equities, on par with bonds.

But cash yields are fleeting: Cash investments are short-term loans to various entities. If interest rates drift down, the high yields may disappear as higher interest rate loans are retired. If you lock in a longer-term CD, you can benefit from that high yield longer. But if you’re in a money market mutual fund or high-yield savings account, your yield will fluctuate based on the prevailing interest rate environment.

Another consideration is inflation risk. Over very long periods, cash yields sometimes beat inflation, but not always. That risk is top of mind for investors as we’ve had above-average inflation recently. Because your long-term yield and return from cash typically will be lower than it is from bonds, inflation will take a bigger bite out of your payout.

I can get a 5% yield on a cash account, and I’m not risking any principal. Why would I bother buying bonds?

items.title: Do this crucial thing to thrive during unemployment
items.summary:
A job search , whatever the length, is demoralizing .

After losing a job, you’ll start asking yourself challenging questions about finances, childcare and more. You may also feel the pang of an identity crisis—particularly if you’re a longtime employee whose daily life has become tied up with work.

On top of that, there’s the hours of applying, networking, interviewing, and dealing with modern-day job hunt maladies, from AI and ghost jobs . Lack of communication and recruiter bait-and-switch make the process feel useless. 

The mental battle can be a monster. But experts suggest a possible sanity-saving sword to slay that monster: the power of having a routine. That can be key, especially when navigating a process that may drag on past six months or more .

Melissa Dorman, an organizational psychologist and executive coach, shares that in today’s anonymous market, “no matter how much you get done, you can feel behind or get sucked into the vortex of applying for one job after another.”

Crafting (and sticking) to a routine during this period is not only a way to stay positive during a job search—but it could also be a means to open up job seekers to new opportunities.

Routines and productivity 

The salve to some of this strangeness may come down to how seekers control what is within their power. A routine can serve as that support and stability that can put a period of uncontrollable unpredictability into perspective.

items.title: A new start after 60: I was burnt out and facing redundancy. So I set up a bee farm – and learned the joys of a simple life
items.summary:
Jeff Lee had spent decades as an investigative journalist. But when he upped sticks with his wife to buy a farm in rural British Columbia, he didn’t just change jobs – he found a different way to live

Jeff Lee became interested in beekeeping in his late 50s after his wife, Amanda, took part in a “beard of bees” event at Science World’s “science of fear” exhibition in Vancouver, Canada, where they lived. She stepped into a Perspex booth, a caged queen bee was placed beneath her chin and thousands of bees climbed her neck – hence the “beard”. She was so calm that the stallholder was impressed. “You should keep bees,” he said.

Lee had a small collection of books on the insects – “the idea of homesteading and having something of an independent life, rather than a rat-race life, always appealed to me” – and the pair enrolled on a beekeeping course. Before long, they had put two hives in their back yard. Fast-forward to 60 and he and Amanda had moved 300 miles east to rural British Columbia to buy a bee farm. For Lee’s part, however, he didn’t just acquire a business. The bees taught him a completely different way to live.
